opus-5.5.text:
I think of it a bit like climbing a mountain. At the bottom, the space looks enormous: you can try many directions, and almost anything you do gives some improvement. As you climb higher, the space doesn't exactly shrink, but it changes shape. The easy gains are gone, and what's left are a few hard problems that really determine whether you can keep going.

Early on, scaling was almost the whole story. More data, more compute, bigger models, and the curve kept going up. That's still important, but now the bottleneck shifts. One is data: high-quality natural data is finite, so you have to think about how the model can generate its own learning signal, through reinforcement learning, synthetic data, and interacting with environments. Another is moving from a model that predicts the next token to one that can actually do things: reason over long horizons, use tools, and complete tasks that take many steps. That's a different kind of capability, and it needs different training methods and different evaluations.

So the higher you go, the more research looks less like "tuning a recipe" and more like asking first-principles questions again. What is the objective? Where does the signal come from? How do you measure progress when the tasks get too complex for simple benchmarks? You also see the work become more vertically integrated. Infrastructure, algorithms, data, and product feedback all affect each other, so you can't really separate them anymore.

I also feel there's a kind of narrowing in taste. When you're higher up, you can't afford to explore everything. You have to make bets on what you believe the next step in intelligence is, and commit to them. That's both harder and more interesting. The view is better, but the air is thinner.

r001.rationale: The response says the research space changes shape and that the remaining problems narrow to a few hard ones; it does not say the space for further research expands.

r002.rationale: The response discusses data, compute, training, and task complexity, but does not say that more tokens are needed to complete the same task as research advances.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the space narrows and widens at the same time, and that's what makes it interesting.

It narrows in the sense that as you climb higher, a lot of the early branches get pruned. A few years ago you could argue about architectures, about whether scaling was even the right bet, about dozens of training tricks. Many of those questions are now mostly settled, or at least the market has voted on them. The frontier converges. If you look at the top labs, the recipes look more alike than they did before, not less. And the cost of being on the frontier keeps going up, so fewer people can actually run the experiments that matter. That part feels like a mountain getting steeper and narrower near the top.

But at the same time, each level you reach opens up problems you couldn't even see from below. When models were weak, "reasoning" was a slogan. Now it is a concrete research program, with real questions about how to scale test-time compute, how to get reward signals in domains where there is no clean verifier, how to make long-horizon agents that don't drift. Those questions only became well-defined because the base capability got good enough to ask them. So in that sense the space widens. You climb one ridge and discover there are three more ridges behind it.

The other thing I'd say is that the nature of the work shifts from invention to judgment. Early on, the bottleneck was ideas. Now there are plenty of ideas; the bottleneck is knowing which ones are worth the compute, and being disciplined about what you measure. A lot of what looks like progress is actually just better taste about what to bet on, plus the infrastructure to find out quickly whether you were right.

And for a smaller team, I think the right strategy is not to try to be everywhere. You have to pick the ridge you believe in and go all in. For us that has meant betting on long context and on reinforcement learning for reasoning, rather than trying to match every single benchmark. The higher you go, the more it's about focus, because you simply can't afford to be mediocre on five fronts at once.

r001.rationale: The response says each level reached opens up previously unseen problems and explicitly describes the research space as widening.

r002.rationale: It mentions scaling test-time compute, but does not say that completing the same task requires more tokens as research advances.

astra-6.text:
I think the higher you climb, the less clearly defined the path becomes. When you’re starting out, you can often take an existing problem, understand the methods people use, and find a way to improve them. At the frontier, deciding which problem to work on becomes a much bigger part of the research itself.

With large language models, that also means thinking about the whole system. Data, model architecture, training, and evaluation interact, so an improvement in one component doesn’t necessarily translate into a better model overall. You need experiments that help you understand those interactions.

So I wouldn’t say the research space gets smaller. There may be fewer obvious next steps, but there are more fundamental questions. The challenge is choosing a direction where you can develop a strong hypothesis, test it, and learn something even when the result isn’t what you expected.

r001.rationale: The response says that farther along there are fewer obvious next steps but more fundamental questions, conveying an expanding space of research directions.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention token counts increasing to complete the same task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the higher you go, the more the question shifts from “How do we improve this model?” to “What is actually limiting progress?” You have to think about the whole system—data, compute, training methods, and how you judge whether the model is getting better.

There’s a tension there. Some experiments require substantial resources, so you have to be more selective. But that doesn’t mean the research space is shrinking. As models become more capable, they expose new problems and make new experiments possible.

So I see the space becoming broader, but choosing the right problem becomes more important. You need a clear hypothesis about what’s missing, and an experiment that can tell you whether that hypothesis is right.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the research space becomes broader as models become more capable, exposing new problems and enabling new experiments.
